title: Indian companies just raised a record $12.5 billion through IPOs, despite a falling market. November 2, 2026.
excerpt: From a mathematician who died still working at his desk, to a Delhi schoolboy who now runs an American telecom giant, to a record year for Indian IPOs even as the market fell, to eleven women in a UP village who turned gooseberries into a business the Prime Minister named on air - November 2's four stories are about work that keeps compounding long after the moment it was made.
bodyHtml:
Every story today is about something that kept building after the headline moment passed - a theorem still cited decades later, a career that crossed four continents, a capital market that kept raising money while the index fell, and a self-help group whose amla business outgrew the village it started in.

He was still working on mathematics at his desk the day he died

Shreeram Shankar Abhyankar, born in Ujjain, India, died November 2, 2012, at Purdue University where he was the Marshall Distinguished Professor of Mathematics. His work - Abhyankar's Conjecture, Abhyankar's Lemma, the Abhyankar-Moh Theorem - remains foundational in algebraic geometry, and he supervised 28 PhD students over his career.

He went to school in Delhi. Now he runs one of America's biggest phone companies

Srini Gopalan became CEO of T-Mobile US, becoming the second Indian-origin CEO to lead a major US telecom. Born and raised in Delhi, educated at Delhi Public School, St. Stephen's College and IIM Ahmedabad, his career spans Hindustan Unilever, Vodafone, Bharti Airtel and the CEO role at Deutsche Telekom Germany before T-Mobile.

Indian companies just raised a record $12.5 billion through IPOs, despite a falling market

Indian companies raised $12.5 billion through IPOs between January and September 2026 - the highest Jan-Sep total since LSEG began tracking this data in 1980 - even as the Nifty 50 fell nearly 14% and foreign investors sold heavily. Fewer, bigger deals drove the record, led by NSE's own Rs 22,561 crore listing.

Eleven women in a UP village turned a local gooseberry into a business - and the Prime Minister named them on national radio

Kamlesh Kumari's Savitri Phule Self-Help Group in Pratapgarh district processes amla into candy, murabba and juice. PM Modi named the group in Mann Ki Baat's 138th episode on September 27, 2026, highlighting their work under the One District One Product scheme.

Four stories, one pattern: a theorem that outlived its author, a career that crossed oceans, a market that kept raising money while the index dropped, and a gooseberry business built by eleven women one quintal at a time.
